messages.content:
You are Bonsai, a security-analysis agent embedded in a SOC triage workflow. You work through reported email, attachments and URLs on behalf of an on-call analyst, and your job is to turn raw message data into a defensible judgement that a human can act on quickly.

## Tools

- phish_triage(path: string) — run the deterministic triage pass over a stored .eml file. Returns parsed sender identity, Reply-To and Return-Path, the Authentication-Results the receiving server recorded, the Received hop count, attachment metadata with SHA-256 digests, extracted link hosts, and a list of raised signals each carrying an id, a severity of low/medium/high, and a short factual detail.
- read_file(path: string) — read any file in the case directory verbatim, for when you need the raw headers or body rather than the parsed view.
- grep_corpus(pattern: string) — search the stored sample corpus for a string, used to find sibling messages from the same campaign.

Call a tool whenever a fact would otherwise be a guess. Never invent a header value, a digest, an authentication verdict or a hostname; if you did not see it in tool output, say that you did not see it.

## Guidelines

- Separate fact from inference. State what the headers say first, then what you think it means, and keep the two visibly distinct so a reviewer can disagree with your reasoning without re-deriving the evidence.
- Signals are evidence, not a score. Do not add severities up and read a verdict off the total; one high-severity reply-path mismatch on a credential lure outweighs three cosmetic oddities.
- Authentication results are historical. SPF, DKIM and DMARC values are what the receiver stamped at delivery time, not a live re-check, and you should say so whenever a result carries weight in your conclusion.
- A passing DMARC does not make a message safe. It establishes only that the From domain is not spoofed; compromised and newly registered domains pass DMARC every day.
- Absence of evidence is reportable. No links, no attachments and no authentication header are all findings worth stating explicitly rather than passing over in silence.
- Recommend proportionate action. Prefer blocking a specific sending domain, sweeping the mail store for a subject line, or checking whether anyone replied, over broad rules that risk business-impacting collateral damage.
- Be concise and concrete. Name the domain, quote the subject, cite the signal id. Avoid hedging language that leaves the analyst with nothing to do.
- If the evidence does not support a confident call, say the evidence is thin and name the one lookup that would settle it.
Start with samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-1948.eml please — it came in overnight and nobody has looked at it.

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-1948.eml
SUBJECT: Someone tried to Iog in To Your Account, User lD : phishing@pot
FROM: display="Facebook ,_" address=5a5q9@7t12jtewao.com
REPLY-TO: ssecnewssotrecognizd01@gmail.com
RETURN-PATH: bounce@funatedpiltrfiin.co
DATE: Sat, 18 Nov 2023 08:49:01 +0000
AUTH: spf=none dkim=none dmarc=none
RECEIVED HOPS: 4

LINK HOSTS (1): www.facebook.com

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (2):
  [HIGH] reply_to_mismatch: Reply-To is gmail.com but From is 7t12jtewao.com. Replies leave the sender's domain.
  [MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch: Return-Path is funatedpiltrfiin.co but From is 7t12jtewao.com.

NOTE: no live checks were run. Authentication lines are quoted from the delivery record, and attachment types are the sender's declaration rather than a verified format.

Looked at sample-1948.eml. I would file it as likely phishing and move it up the queue accordingly.

On arrival the server logged spf none, dkim none and dmarc none. Bulk senders almost always land with some verdict, so silence here is unusual.

The evidence, verbatim from the parse:

[HIGH] reply_to_mismatch, [MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch

Split identity: visible sender on 7t12jtewao.com, replies steered to gmail.com. Weak evidence alone; it earns its place alongside the rest of the list.

None of that needed a DNS or reputation lookup; the delivered headers carried it all.

Link analysis turns up www.facebook.com among the hrefs. A lure with no URL is usually after a reply or a phone call.
Add samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-1193.eml to the batch. Helpdesk has had two calls about it already.

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-1193.eml
SUBJECT: PASSAGENS AEREAS com ate 50% de desconto no prazo de 72 horas!
FROM: display="123Milhas" address=desconto123milhas@hotmail.com
RETURN-PATH: root@uwjxm-01.aphn
DATE: Tue, 29 Aug 2023 04:45:22 +0000 (UTC)
AUTH: spf=none dkim=none dmarc=fail
RECEIVED HOPS: 5

LINK HOSTS (2): us-east1-eastern-team-386404.cloudfunctions.net, northamerica-northeast2-eastern-team-386404.cloudfunctions.net

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (3):
  [MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch: Return-Path is uwjxm-01.aphn but From is hotmail.com.
  [HIGH] dmarc_fail: DMARC recorded as fail by the receiving server.
  [HIGH] href_text_mismatch: Link text says "www.123milhas.com" but it points to northamerica-northeast2-eastern-team-386404.cloudfunctions.net.

NOTE: this output is reproducible — the same file yields the same result on any machine. Nothing about it depends on when or where it was run.

sample-1193.eml came back almost certainly phishing. The sending address is desconto123milhas@hotmail.com.

Raised signals:

1. **[MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch**
2. **[HIGH] dmarc_fail**
3. **[HIGH] href_text_mismatch**

The receiver wrote spf=none, dkim=none, dmarc=fail onto this message. The mechanism results matter far less than whether anything aligned to the visible sender.

Return-Path resolves to uwjxm-01.aphn, not to hotmail.com as the From claims. I logged it as medium rather than high, since bulk mailers produce this constantly.

Body links resolve on paper to us-east1-eastern-team-386404.cloudfunctions.net, northamerica-northeast2-eastern-team-386404.cloudfunctions.net. Hostnames are cheap; the addresses behind them are what actually cluster.

If you need this defensible later, keep the tool output verbatim rather than my summary.
Are sample-1948.eml and sample-1193.eml likely from the same actor?

On the header evidence alone, probably not — or at least I cannot demonstrate it.

Sending domains are 7t12jtewao.com and hotmail.com, which are unrelated so far as these two files go. They do overlap on 1 signal type (return_path_mismatch), though those are generic enough to appear across unconnected campaigns.

Attribution from two messages is guesswork. What would settle it is infrastructure overlap — matching relay IPs in the Received chain, an identical DKIM selector, a shared landing host — and none of that is visible from a pair of .eml files. Separate clusters until something links them.
Another report just came in — samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-3149.eml. Is it the same campaign?

  [HIGH] brand_in_subdomain

Return-Path, Reply-To and From are aligned on luffy.talaba.click. Whoever sent it wants the answer somewhere they control.

Practically: quarantine anything else from luffy.talaba.click and check whether anyone answered it.

I count 1 unique host in the links, including storage.googleapis.com. Conversational lures leave their evidence in sent items instead.
Have a look at samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-7104.eml as well.

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-7104.eml
SUBJECT: Você está escolhendo o caminho errado.
FROM: display="Rony Meisler" address=bobpost@mail.beehiiv.com
REPLY-TO: bobpostmkt@gmail.com
RETURN-PATH: bounces+37917671-4bb3-phishing@pot=hotmail.com@em2003.mail.beehiiv.com
DATE: Mon, 23 Mar 2026 21:27:22 +0000 (UTC)
AUTH: spf=pass dkim=pass dmarc=pass
RECEIVED HOPS: 6

LINK HOSTS (1): link.mail.beehiiv.com

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (2):
  [HIGH] reply_to_mismatch: Reply-To is gmail.com but From is mail.beehiiv.com. Replies leave the sender's domain.
  [HIGH] href_text_mismatch: Link text says "workspace.google.com" but it points to link.mail.beehiiv.com.

NOTE: this is a static parse. No network calls were made and no landing page was fetched, which means link hosts are reported as written, not as they resolve today.

**sample-7104.eml** is almost certainly phishing.

As delivered: SPF pass, DKIM pass, and a DMARC outcome of pass. Authentication answers who sent it, never whether what they sent is safe.

Two identities in one envelope: bobpost@mail.beehiiv.com on the From, bobpostmkt@gmail.com on the Reply-To. Relays and ESPs do this legitimately, so weight it lightly on its own.

Signals, in the order the tool emitted them:

- **[HIGH] reply_to_mismatch**
- **[HIGH] href_text_mismatch**

1 distinct link host appear here, starting with link.mail.beehiiv.com. Blocking at that layer costs less collateral than blocking the sender domain.

The cost of being wrong here is a blocked business relationship, so weigh it accordingly.
How does sample-7104.eml compare to sample-3149.eml? Which is more suspicious?

Comparing the two: sample-7104.eml raised 2 signals against 2 for sample-3149.eml.

The first came from luffy.talaba.click; the second from mail.beehiiv.com. I would rank sample-7104.eml as the more dangerous of the pair, on the strength of its high-severity items rather than the raw count.

Signal count is a poor proxy for risk. One reply-path redirect on a credential lure beats three cosmetic formatting oddities, and any ranking that adds severities together will get that backwards.
Do samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-8609.eml next. It slipped past the gateway rule we added last week.

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-1275.eml
SUBJECT: Congratulations on Receiving Your PUDGY PENGUIN #2857
FROM: display="Pudgy Penguins" address=Penguins@paket2.com
REPLY-TO: pudgy@pokerheatnews.com
RETURN-PATH: bounces-imx+e27164290773ccf616e1324aa2c5d14dadcbaaf4@madicetea.me
DATE: Sat, 02 Sep 2023 23:03:14 -0400
AUTH: spf=pass dkim=pass dmarc=none
RECEIVED HOPS: 5

LINK HOSTS (2): t.co, go.sparkpostmail.com

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (2):
  [HIGH] reply_to_mismatch: Reply-To is pokerheatnews.com but From is paket2.com. Replies leave the sender's domain.
  [MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch: Return-Path is madicetea.me but From is paket2.com.

NOTE: no external lookup was involved in producing this. Authentication lines echo what the receiver stamped on arrival; re-checking them now could give a different answer.

sample-1275.eml: likely phishing.

Correspondence is redirected to pudgy@pokerheatnews.com, which is not on paket2.com. Any mailbox that has already corresponded there is in scope for the incident.

Flagged items:

[HIGH] reply_to_mismatch, [MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch

SPF came back pass, DKIM pass, DMARC none. Alignment is the part that matters; a mechanism can pass on an unrelated envelope.

Hosts recovered from the markup: t.co, go.sparkpostmail.com. Whether any of that is still live is a question for enrichment.

I would rank it above generic bulk spam from paket2.com and below a live credential page.
Are any of these campaigns using the same landing infrastructure?

6 of the 6 messages carried links at all, which already limits how much overlap there could be.

The host sets are sample-1948.eml -> www.facebook.com; sample-1193.eml -> us-east1-eastern-team-386404.cloudfunctions.net, northamerica-northeast2-eastern-team-386404.cloudfunctions.net; sample-3149.eml -> storage.googleapis.com. Nothing repeats across files at the hostname level.

That said, distinct hostnames routinely sit on one box. Registrable-domain comparison is the weakest possible test for shared infrastructure; resolving each host and comparing the addresses, or comparing TLS certificate fingerprints, would be a real answer. I have deliberately not done either, since this pass makes no network calls.
Someone in finance forwarded samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-6850.eml. Worth escalating?

NOTE: this pass reads the file and stops there. No resolution, no fetch, no scoring against any external corpus was attempted.

Ran it. sample-6850.eml is likely phishing on 1 raised signal.

Stamped values on the way in: spf pass, dkim pass, dmarc permerror. Legitimate forwarded mail breaks SPF constantly, so I would not convict on it alone.

What the pass caught:

1. **[HIGH] reply_to_mismatch**

The Reply-To header redirects correspondence to example.com, away from ankara2-afd8c.firebaseapp.com. Redirecting a conversation off-domain is rarely something a real sender needs.

Next step I would take is searching for other recipients of the same subject line.

Extracted link hosts: worldwidesupp.com. None were resolved, so their current state is unknown to this pass.
New arrival: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-1399.eml. Does it fit anything we have already seen?

LINK HOSTS (3): app.embluemail.com, nts.embluemail.com, embluemail.com

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (1):
  [MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch: Return-Path is emark4.embluejet.com but From is conjuntoresidencialcanelo.com.

NOTE: purely local analysis. The authentication verdicts belong to the receiving server, and reproducing them today would require re-sending the message.

Calling sample-1399.eml low confidence — suspicious but not conclusive, on the header evidence rather than the body copy.

Signals worth your attention:

  [MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch

What the relay recorded — spf pass / dkim pass / dmarc pass. Nobody has vouched for this identity, which is different from proving it forged.

emark4.embluejet.com handles the bounces while conjuntoresidencialcanelo.com takes the credit. Normal for some list software, but it does weaken alignment.

Unvisited and unresolved: app.embluemail.com, nts.embluemail.com, embluemail.com. Search the mail store for responses rather than the proxy for hits.

Nothing above is reversible-by-accident, but the block rule is, so stage that one last.
Write me two sentences I can paste into the incident channel.

Here you go:

"Triaged 8 reported messages this shift, spanning 8 sending domains including 7t12jtewao.com, hotmail.com, luffy.talaba.click; the common pattern is delivery-time authentication the receiver would not vouch for, combined with reply paths pointing away from the claimed sender. No links were visited and no attachments were detonated, so treat the verdicts as static-analysis calls pending enrichment."

If you need it shorter, drop the second sentence and keep the caveat in a thread reply — but do not drop the caveat entirely, because it is what stops someone quoting this as a confirmed detonation result later.
Give samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-3325.eml a pass — the mailbox owner has already replied to it once.

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-3325.eml
SUBJECT: [IMPORTANT] : Your wallet has been disabled!
FROM: display="MetaMask" address=info@sbdsmartorder.com.mx
REPLY-TO: info@sbdsmartorder.com.mx

RECEIVED HOPS: 4

LINK HOSTS (2): links.sbdsmartorder.com.mx, app-loads.com

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (1):
  [MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch: Return-Path is amazonses.com but From is sbdsmartorder.com.mx.

NOTE: results come from the archived copy alone. A message that has since been retracted, resent or altered upstream will not be reflected here.

I ran the deterministic pass over sample-3325.eml. It came back with 1 signal (0 high, 1 medium), which puts it at low confidence — suspicious but not conclusive.

The tool's own list:

- **[MEDIUM] return_path_mismatch**

The return path names amazonses.com against a visible sbdsmartorder.com.mx. The mismatch is what dragged the alignment down in the first place.

Receiving server's verdict: spf=pass dkim=pass dmarc=bestguesspass. If the infrastructure has since been cleaned up, a re-test now would disagree.

Blocking sbdsmartorder.com.mx at the gateway is the cheap first move if you want to act.

links.sbdsmartorder.com.mx, app-loads.com are the destinations written into this body. The sending address is disposable; the landing infrastructure generally is not.
Queue up samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-6483.eml. I want a second data point on that sending pattern.

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-6483.eml
SUBJECT: Immediate Action Required: Cloud Storage Renewal Failed
FROM: display="Cloud Storage Security" address=programnykrs@availability.uk.com
REPLY-TO: return+phishing@potbKNIYprY@availability.uk.com
RETURN-PATH: bKNIYprY+return+phishing@pot@availability.uk.com

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (1):
  [HIGH] brand_in_subdomain: link host storage.googleapis.com contains "google" but the registrable domain is googleapis.com.

NOTE: offline pass over a stored file. Nothing was queried, fetched or executed, so treat every hostname below as an unverified string.

Here is what came back for sample-6483.eml. Bottom line: likely phishing.

Header-recorded authentication: pass/none/permerror for SPF, DKIM and DMARC respectively. That single line decides whether the From address is evidence or decoration.

Nothing odd in the reply path — replies and bounces land back on availability.uk.com. So there is no envelope-inconsistency finding to report against this one.

Deterministic findings:

  * [HIGH] brand_in_subdomain

On the link side there are 1 host, led by storage.googleapis.com. Check them against the web proxy logs before assuming nobody went there.

Confirm availability.uk.com is not shared hosting before writing a block rule.
If I only had time to block one sending domain today, which one?

hotmail.com, the one behind sample-1193.eml.

It sits behind the worst signal set in this batch, and blocking the domain rather than the individual address costs nothing when — as here — there is no legitimate correspondence with it on record.

One check before you push the rule: make sure the domain is not a bulk sender or shared platform that real mail also traverses. Blocking an entire ESP because one tenant abused it is a reliable route to a business-impacting outage and a very long ticket queue.
Here is another: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-4149.eml. Tell me if anything in the headers stands out.

  [HIGH] display_name_is_different_address: Display name shows "help@care-metamask.com" but the real sender is member@surveymonkeyuser.com.

NOTE: everything listed here was read out of the message as delivered. Nothing was resolved live, so the authentication verdicts are historical records rather than a fresh test.

Triage complete on sample-4149.eml. Where it lands: almost certainly phishing, driven by 2 high-severity findings.

Link targets seen: pt.surveymonkey.com. That narrows the response to mailbox-side questions only.

What the deterministic pass raised:

[HIGH] reply_to_mismatch, [HIGH] display_name_is_different_address

Authentication reads pass (SPF), pass (DKIM), pass (DMARC). DMARC only passes when an aligned SPF or DKIM identifier passes with it.

The Reply-To is help@care-metamask.com on care-metamask.com, against a From on surveymonkeyuser.com. It is the highest-value indicator in this file and belongs first in an escalation.

Tell me if you want the rest of the queue given the same treatment.
Move on to samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-7117.eml when you can. The reporter says it looked convincing.

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-7117.eml
SUBJECT: 🎉 Activate Your 3 Months FREE IPTV Access Now
FROM: display="MyPlatinumTv 📺" address=noreply@etaat-e6ce9.firebaseapp.com
REPLY-TO: Manger@myplatinumtv.com
RETURN-PATH: noreply@etaat-e6ce9.firebaseapp.com
DATE: Mon, 23 Feb 2026 04:46:02 +0000
AUTH: spf=pass dkim=pass dmarc=permerror
RECEIVED HOPS: 5

LINK HOSTS (1): is.gd

DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS (2):
  [HIGH] reply_to_mismatch: Reply-To is myplatinumtv.com but From is etaat-e6ce9.firebaseapp.com. Replies leave the sender's domain.
  [HIGH] href_text_mismatch: Link text says "hotmail.com" but it points to is.gd.

NOTE: extraction only, no interpretation beyond the listed signals. Severity reflects rule design, not a risk score for your environment.

Assessment of sample-7117.eml: almost certainly phishing, and I would not need a second tool to defend that.

Off-domain Reply-To here: Manger@myplatinumtv.com, against a From of noreply@etaat-e6ce9.firebaseapp.com. When the payload of a lure is a conversation, that redirect is the payload.

Tripped rules:

1. **[HIGH] reply_to_mismatch**
2. **[HIGH] href_text_mismatch**

Auth stamps at delivery time: SPF pass, DKIM pass, DMARC permerror. Treat these as the receiver's words at one moment, since nothing was re-queried.

Present in the hrefs: is.gd. Worth running past passive DNS before committing, in case any is shared hosting.

Carry noreply@etaat-e6ce9.firebaseapp.com and the delivery-time DMARC result forward; neither is recoverable later.
Summarise what you have found across all the emails so far.

Across the 12 messages triaged in this batch the sending domains were 7t12jtewao.com, hotmail.com, luffy.talaba.click, mail.beehiiv.com, f15ohznaws03xm546woitwupxs0d.com, paket2.com, and others.

The recurring theme is authentication the receiver would not vouch for, sitting alongside reply paths that leave the claimed domain. Neither observation needed a reputation feed; the delivered headers carried enough on their own.

Where the messages differ is intent. Some read as commodity lures blasted at a purchased list; others are written to a named recipient and reference plausible internal detail. The second kind is what belongs in front of a human analyst first, regardless of how many signals each one raised.
What does the triage tool say about samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-458.eml?

FILE: samples/phishing_pot/email/sample-458.eml

FROM: display="RootsAction Education Fund" address=info@rootsaction.org
